indications.drug:
Ischemic heart disease and angina
definitions
indications.text: Ischemic heart disease is an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand (decreased blood flow to tissue, so too little oxygen). Coronary heart disease is atherosclerotic narrowing of one or more coronary arteries. Angina pectoris (chest pain) is the clinical manifestation of myocardial ischemia.
indications.edu: Angina is the symptom; ischemia, supply falling short of demand, is the cause. Acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina, acute myocardial infarction, sudden cardiac death) is the dangerous end; chronic stable angina is the predictable one.
verify: Imbalance between myocardial O2 supply and demand
Atherosclerotic narrowing of one or more coronary arteries

indications.drug:
Antianginal strategy
what every drug is trying to do
indications.text: Lower myocardial oxygen demand (lower heart rate, lower contractility, lower intramyocardial wall tension by reducing preload and afterload) and raise oxygen supply (improve coronary blood flow). Also stabilize atherosclerotic plaques to prevent acute coronary syndrome and modify reversible risk factors.
indications.edu: Place every drug on this map: beta blockers lower demand only; calcium channel blockers and nitrates lower demand and help supply; statins, antiplatelets and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are the vasculoprotective group.
verify: Stabilize atherosclerotic plaques to prevent ACS
Mild dilation in areas of fixed stenosis

indications.drug:
Three treatment pillars
revascularization, drugs, lifestyle
indications.text: Revascularization (percutaneous coronary intervention, coronary artery bypass grafting); pharmacotherapy: antianginals (beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, nitrates) plus vasculoprotective drugs (antiplatelet, statins, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors); lifestyle change of modifiable risk factors.
indications.edu: The antianginals are the symptom drugs; antiplatelets and lipid-lowering therapy are for every patient who can take them; angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are for diabetes, left ventricular dysfunction or a prior infarction.

indications.drug:
Antianginal classes
what they accomplish
indications.text: Antianginals improve exercise capacity, reduce exercise-induced ST-segment changes and decrease the frequency of symptoms. The three classes are beta blockers, calcium channel blockers (dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine) and nitrates.
indications.edu: Expect the patient to report longer time to chest pain with exertion and fewer attacks.

indications.drug:
Variant (Prinzmetal) angina
vasospastic angina
indications.text: Transient, abrupt narrowing of the vessel, which can occur at a partly occluded site and may be due to autonomic control. Younger patients and those with fewer risk factors; with or without ST-segment elevation; often at night or in the early morning.
indications.edu: The pattern to recognize: younger patient, few risk factors, chest pain at night or early morning.
verify: Younger patient and those with fewer risk factors
Often occurs during the night or early morning hours

indications.drug:
Variant angina treatment
calcium channel blockers and nitrates
indications.text: Calcium channel blockers and nitrates can reduce symptoms.
indications.edu: Beta blockers are the exception: avoid them, because they may lead to worsened symptoms. The usual first-line antianginal is the wrong drug here.
verify: Calcium channel blockers and nitrates can reduce symptoms

indications.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
indications.text: First-line therapy for angina in the absence of contraindications. Useful when the patient has limited exercise capacity due to angina and also has hypertension, anxiety, supraventricular arrhythmias, stable (compensated) heart failure or a prior myocardial infarction. Either beta-1 selective (metoprolol, atenolol) or non-selective (propranolol, nadolol) agents may be used; third-generation agents are carvedilol and labetalol.
indications.edu: The class is the default, and the coexisting conditions in the list are the clues that point to it. Acute decompensated heart failure is a contraindication.
verify: First line therapy in the absence of contraindications
Useful for patients with limited exercise capacity due to angina, HTN, anxiety, supraventricular arrhythmias, heart-failure, post-MI

indications.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
indications.text: Monitoring: heart rate, blood sugar and lipids.
indications.edu: These three follow from the adverse effects: slow pulse, raised glucose and altered lipids.

indications.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
indications.text: Patient education: avoid rapid discontinuation; expect dizziness and fatigue.
indications.edu: Never stop a beta blocker suddenly; stop gradually. (Added background: abrupt cessation can cause rebound angina and myocardial infarction.)

indications.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
indications.text: Comorbid conditions: the first-line antianginal is a beta blocker when the patient has hypertension, a prior myocardial infarction or decreased left ventricular function.
indications.edu: Prior myocardial infarction is also the trigger in the treatment summary: beta blockers are given after an infarction unless contraindicated.
verify: Prior myocardial infarction: first line beta blocker
Decreased left ventricular function: first line beta blocker

indications.drug:
Calcium channel blockers
dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine
indications.text: Place in therapy: non-dihydropyridine agents are initial therapy when beta blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated. Dihydropyridine agents are added in combination with a beta blocker when the beta blocker alone is not successful. Calcium channel blockers may also be combined with long-acting nitrates.
indications.edu: Drug selection rule: non-dihydropyridine for initial therapy; dihydropyridine when combined with a beta blocker.
verify: Initial therapy for reduction of symptoms when beta blockers are contraindicated or are not tolerated (NDHP)
In combination with beta blockers when initial treatment with beta blockers is not successful (DHP)
DHP when combined with beta blocker

indications.drug:
Calcium channel blockers
dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine
indications.text: Calcium channel blockers (as a class) are chosen for: patients who cannot take or do not tolerate beta blockers, vasospastic angina, severe peripheral vascular disease, asthma and uncontrolled diabetes. Left ventricular dysfunction applies to dihydropyridines only (amlodipine).
indications.edu: These are the patients for whom a calcium channel blocker takes the place of a beta blocker.
verify: Contraindications/intolerance to beta blockers, vasospastic angina, severe peripheral vascular disease, asthma, uncontrolled diabetes

indications.drug:
Calcium channel blockers
dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine
indications.text: Choosing inside the class: diltiazem and verapamil (non-dihydropyridines) give moderate vasodilation and slow the heart and atrioventricular conduction; nifedipine, amlodipine and felodipine (dihydropyridines) give the strongest vasodilation and leave atrioventricular conduction unchanged.
indications.edu: The exact plus counts are not the point: non-dihydropyridines act on the heart and the vessels; dihydropyridines act mainly on the vessels.

indications.drug:
Calcium channel blockers
dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine
indications.text: Monitoring: relief of symptoms, and heart rate for the non-dihydropyridines. Education: dizziness and constipation (constipation mainly with verapamil).
indications.edu: Avoid short-acting agents, nifedipine being the named example. Warn about dizziness and constipation.

indications.drug:
Short-acting nitrates
nitroglycerin: sublingual tablet (Nitrostat), lingual spray (Nitrolingual Pumpspray)
indications.text: Goals of therapy: relieve acute symptoms of myocardial ischemia and prevent effort-induced angina. The treatment summary gives sublingual nitroglycerin for acute relief.
indications.edu: These are the rescue medicines, taken at the first sign of an attack or before a known trigger such as exertion.
verify: To relieve acute symptoms of myocardial ischemia

indications.drug:
Short-acting nitrates
nitroglycerin: sublingual tablet (Nitrostat), lingual spray (Nitrolingual Pumpspray)
indications.text: If the first dose gives no relief after 5 minutes, call emergency medical services. (Further doses may be taken at 5-minute intervals while waiting for help, usually up to three doses in total; this ceiling is standard practice.)
indications.edu: A patient who still has chest pain 5 minutes after the first dose may be having a myocardial infarction: the action is to call for help, not to wait.
verify: Dosed every 5 minutes until relief or EMS arrives
Call EMS if no relief 5 minutes after first dose

indications.drug:
Short-acting nitrates
nitroglycerin: sublingual tablet (Nitrostat), lingual spray (Nitrolingual Pumpspray)
indications.text: Storage: keep in the original packaging in a cool, dry place; traditional counseling is to replace the tablets 3–6 months after opening (current labeling gives the printed expiration date if the tablets stay in the tightly closed original glass container), and to replace them sooner if they no longer work. Administration: the tablet or spray is applied under the tongue.
indications.edu: A patient who says the tablets no longer work should be asked how old the bottle is and how it was stored.
verify: Store in original packaging, cool dry place
Apply or spray under the tongue

indications.drug:
Short-acting nitrates
nitroglycerin: sublingual tablet (Nitrostat), lingual spray (Nitrolingual Pumpspray)
indications.text: Warn about orthostatic hypotension (dizziness or fainting on standing).
indications.edu: Warn the patient to expect possible dizziness on standing after a dose.

indications.drug:
Long-acting nitrates
isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur), isosorbide dinitrate; nitroglycerin ointment (Nitro-Bid) and transdermal patch
indications.text: Place in therapy: initial therapy when beta blockers and calcium channel blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated, or in combination with them when they are not successful. Usually an adjunct; not recommended as monotherapy. Monotherapy is discouraged when a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker can be used; a long-acting nitrate alone is accepted only when neither can be.
indications.edu: A long-acting nitrate is almost never the only antianginal; look for the partner drug in the stem.
verify: Initial therapy for reduction of symptoms when beta blockers and calcium channel blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated

indications.drug:
Long-acting nitrates
isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur), isosorbide dinitrate; nitroglycerin ointment (Nitro-Bid) and transdermal patch
indications.text: Isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur) lasts 12 hours and is dosed once daily. Isosorbide dinitrate lasts 3–6 hours and is dosed three times daily.
indications.edu: The mononitrate is the once-daily agent; the dinitrate is the three-times-daily agent.
verify: Duration 3-6 hours, dosed three times daily

indications.drug:
Long-acting nitrates
isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur), isosorbide dinitrate; nitroglycerin ointment (Nitro-Bid) and transdermal patch
indications.text: Ointment and patch: 12 hours on, 12 hours off. Ointment: squeeze onto the calibrated applicator paper, spread in a thin layer on the chest, keep covered with applicator paper, and wipe off the previous dose before adding a new one. Adverse reactions: headache, flushing, postural hypotension, reflex tachycardia.
indications.edu: The 12-hour break is the nitrate-free interval that prevents tolerance.
verify: Wipe off previous dose before adding new dose
Headache, flushing, postural hypotension, reflex tachycardia

indications.drug:
Nitrates
nitroglycerin, isosorbide
indications.text: Tachyphylaxis (tolerance) develops with continuous nitrate exposure; the mechanism is not fully understood (depletion of cofactors, counter-regulatory responses, plasma volume expansion, decreased enzyme activity). Management: a nitrate-free interval, timed to when the patient has the lowest frequency of symptoms.
indications.edu: Do not give around-the-clock nitrate exposure: build in a daily period without the drug.
verify: Nitrate free interval when patient has lowest symptom frequency

indications.drug:
Nitrates
nitroglycerin, isosorbide
indications.text: Never combine a nitrate with a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil): concurrent use may lead to hypotension, myocardial infarction or stroke.
indications.edu: Ask every patient on a nitrate about erectile dysfunction medicines; this is the classic dangerous nitrate interaction.
verify: Concurrent use may lead to hypotension, MI/stroke

indications.drug:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
used in coronary artery disease
indications.text: Used in coronary artery disease with diabetes and/or left ventricular systolic dysfunction; should be used indefinitely after a myocardial infarction, with left ventricular dysfunction or with diabetes; consider in all patients with coronary artery disease or other vascular disease. They do not significantly affect myocardial oxygen consumption and do not relieve angina; they may help prevent progression of the disease.
indications.edu: Not an antianginal: do not expect chest-pain relief; the benefit is long-term protection.
verify: Used in patients with coronary artery disease with diabetes and/or left ventricular systolic dysfunction
Do not relieve symptoms of angina

indications.drug:
Aspirin
antiplatelet
indications.text: Aspirin in the absence of contraindications for all patients with ischemic heart disease, to prevent acute coronary syndrome.
indications.edu: Aspirin is the default antiplatelet; the question becomes clopidogrel only when aspirin is not an option.
verify: Aspirin in the absence of contraindications
All patients with ischemic heart disease without contraindications
Used to prevent acute coronary syndrome

indications.drug:
Clopidogrel
antiplatelet
indications.text: Recommended for patients allergic to aspirin; as efficacious as aspirin in secondary prevention.
indications.edu: Aspirin allergy is the trigger for choosing clopidogrel in stable ischemic heart disease.
verify: As efficacious as aspirin in secondary prevention
Recommended for patients allergic to aspirin

indications.drug:
Give unless contraindicated
the standard bundle
indications.text: Aspirin; a beta blocker if there was a prior myocardial infarction; an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor in patients with diabetes or left ventricular dysfunction; lipid-lowering therapy; sublingual nitroglycerin for acute relief (symptom relief, not protection).
indications.edu: Match the drug to the trigger: prior infarction points to the beta blocker, diabetes or weak left ventricle to the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
verify: ACEI in patients with DM or LV dysfunction

indications.drug:
Prophylactic antianginals
beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, long-acting nitrates
indications.text: For daily or more frequent symptoms, add prophylactic therapy: beta blockers, calcium channel blockers or long-acting nitrates.
indications.edu: Sublingual nitroglycerin alone is for occasional attacks; daily symptoms call for a preventive drug.
verify: For daily or more frequent symptoms

indications.drug:
Combination therapy
beta blocker plus calcium channel blocker
indications.text: Consider combining when angina persists on one drug. A beta blocker and a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker may be combined if tolerated (some evidence of longer exercise duration); a non-dihydropyridine with a beta blocker is a precaution (the concern is additive heart block and bradycardia, inferred from their heart rate and conduction effects). If a third agent seems needed, the patient probably needs further workup such as angiography.
indications.edu: Persistent symptoms on two drugs usually call for further testing (for example angiography) before a third drug.
verify: Consider if angina persists with monotherapy
May combine BB and CCB if patient can tolerate
In combination with beta blockers when initial treatment with beta blockers is not successful (DHP)

indications.drug:
Acute coronary syndrome
classification
indications.text: ST-elevation myocardial infarction versus non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome, which includes unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. The electrocardiogram (ST elevation or not) sorts the two groups; a biochemical marker separates unstable angina from infarction.
indications.edu: Electrocardiogram first (ST elevation or not), then the blood marker (unstable angina versus infarction).
verify: A biochemical marker separates unstable angina from myocardial infarction

indications.drug:
Goals of therapy
acute coronary syndrome
indications.text: Reestablish coronary blood flow, relieve chest pain, prevent progression to myocardial infarction, prevent heart failure and prevent death.
indications.edu: Each acute drug maps to one goal: fibrinolytics reopen flow, nitrates and morphine relieve pain, aspirin and antithrombotics prevent progression.

indications.drug:
Aspirin
antiplatelet
indications.text: Given at the first signs of chest pain: chew and swallow. Reduces mortality and reinfarction; also decreases recurrent ischemia, stroke and cardiac death. Common to both ST-elevation myocardial infarction and non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome.
indications.edu: Tell the patient to chew and swallow the tablet rather than swallow it whole; it is given at the first sign of chest pain.
verify: used at first signs of chest pain
Common pharmacologic therapy for both STEMI and NSTE ACS
decreased recurrent ischemia, reinfarction, stroke, cardiac death

indications.drug:
Nitrates in acute coronary syndrome
nitroglycerin
indications.text: Sublingual therapy until the patient reaches the hospital, then an intravenous infusion. Benefit: relief of chest pain only, with no mortality benefit.
indications.edu: Nitrates treat the pain, not the outcome; do not pick a nitrate as the drug that lowers mortality.
verify: Start with SL therapy until in the hospital then IV infusion
no mortality benefit, just relief of chest pain

indications.drug: Beta blockers in acute coronary syndrome
indications.text: Started early. Older teaching is intravenous followed by oral therapy; current practice favors oral therapy within the first day and avoids the intravenous route when there is heart failure, low cardiac output or risk of shock. Benefits listed in older trials: smaller infarct size and less sudden cardiac death; the early mortality and heart failure benefits are not established today.
indications.edu: Nitrates relieve pain without an outcome benefit; beta blockers have a long-term outcome benefit after infarction, but only when acute decompensated heart failure, shock risk, heart block and bradycardia are absent.
verify: reduction in early and late mortality, reduction in infarct size

indications.drug:
Morphine
opioid analgesic
indications.text: For chest pain unresponsive to nitrates, used in ST-elevation myocardial infarction. It may increase mortality in unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, and its use is controversial.
indications.edu: It is a second-line pain drug for the ST-elevation group; do not generalize it to unstable angina.
verify: Management of chest pain unresponsive to nitrates
May have increased mortality in UA/NSTEMI

indications.drug:
Fibrinolytics
streptokinase; alteplase (Activase), reteplase (Retavase), tenecteplase (TNKase)
indications.text: For ST-elevation myocardial infarction presenting early (within 12 hours of symptom onset). Less benefit with older age or late presentation; not recommended in non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (bleeding risk exceeds benefit). Relatively few patients receive them. Bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage, is the main risk.
indications.edu: Fibrinolytics belong only to the ST-elevation group; in non-ST-elevation disease they are not used.
verify: Relatively few patients receive these agents

indications.drug:
Fibrinolytics
streptokinase; alteplase (Activase), reteplase (Retavase), tenecteplase (TNKase)
indications.text: Agents named: streptokinase (a bacterial protein, not recombinant); the recombinant tissue plasminogen activators alteplase (Activase), made by recombinant deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) technology in Chinese hamster ovary cells and very expensive; reteplase (Retavase), made in Escherichia coli cells; tenecteplase (TNKase), recombinant with substituted amino acids. Reteplase and tenecteplase have a longer half-life than alteplase.
indications.edu: Brand names to recognize: Activase, Retavase, TNKase.

verify: Streptokinase forms stable 1:1 complex with plasminogen

indications.drug:
Other antithrombotic agents
glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors, P2Y12 receptor antagonists, heparins
indications.text: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors are not routinely recommended before percutaneous coronary intervention. P2Y12 receptor antagonists are used before percutaneous coronary intervention and as clot prophylaxis when a stent is placed. Heparins are used together with fibrinolysis or antiplatelet agents.
indications.edu: Stent placement brings a P2Y12 receptor antagonist; fibrinolysis or antiplatelet therapy brings a heparin.
verify: Not routinely recommended prior to PCI
Used in conjunction with fibrinolysis or antiplatelet agents

indications.drug:
Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome
unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
indications.text: Early treatment is similar to ST-elevation myocardial infarction, but fibrinolytics are not recommended (bleeding risk exceeds benefit). Enoxaparin is preferred over unfractionated heparin (older studies; current guidelines accept either), and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors are used more commonly.
indications.edu: Three differences to remember: no fibrinolytics, enoxaparin over heparin, more glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors.

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
sideeffects.text: Hypotension and bradycardia (slowed pulse) are the listed cardiovascular adverse reactions.
sideeffects.monitor: Monitor heart rate. Warn about dizziness.

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)

Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
sideeffects.text: Fatigue, sexual dysfunction, nightmares and worsened claudication (leg pain on walking from peripheral vascular disease).
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about tiredness, sleep and sexual function; patients with peripheral vascular disease may notice more leg pain.
verify: Fatigue, sexual dysfunction, nightmares, worsened claudication

sideeffects.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
sideeffects.text: Rapid discontinuation must be avoided; stop gradually. (Added background: abrupt cessation can cause rebound angina and myocardial infarction.) Added background: several beta blockers (for example metoprolol, atenolol and nadolol) carry a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) boxed warning (black box) for abrupt cessation; carvedilol and labetalol carry no boxed warning.
sideeffects.monitor: Never stop abruptly; stop gradually. Ask about missed doses, running out of medicine and travel.

sideeffects.drug:
Calcium channel blockers
dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine
sideeffects.text: Hypotension is the adverse reaction listed for the whole class.
sideeffects.monitor: Monitor for relief of symptoms; ask about dizziness on standing.

sideeffects.drug:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about headache and ankle swelling; these come from the vasodilation.

sideeffects.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
sideeffects.text: Slow the heart rate and atrioventricular conduction (verapamil the most), and lower contractility; dihydropyridines leave conduction unchanged.
sideeffects.monitor: Monitor heart rate. Watch for heart block, especially when combined with a beta blocker.

sideeffects.drug:
Calcium channel blockers
dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine
sideeffects.text: Dizziness and constipation are the counseling points for the class; constipation is mainly a verapamil effect.
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about bowel habits and dizziness.

sideeffects.drug:
Long-acting nitrates
isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur), isosorbide dinitrate; nitroglycerin ointment (Nitro-Bid) and transdermal patch
sideeffects.text: Headache, flushing, postural hypotension and reflex tachycardia (a fast pulse as the body answers the fall in pressure).
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about headache and dizziness on standing; orthostatic hypotension is the warning for every nitrate user.
verify: Headache, flushing, postural hypotension, reflex tachycardia

sideeffects.drug:
Short-acting nitrates
nitroglycerin: sublingual tablet (Nitrostat), lingual spray (Nitrolingual Pumpspray)
sideeffects.text: Orthostatic hypotension is the warning given for the short-acting forms.
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about dizziness on standing after a dose.
Use a nitrate-free interval, timed to when symptoms are least frequent.

sideeffects.text: Hypotension and myocardial infarction or stroke when taken with a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil).
sideeffects.monitor: Screen for erectile dysfunction drugs before starting or dosing a nitrate.
verify: Concurrent use may lead to hypotension, MI/stroke

sideeffects.text: Hypotension and allergy. It may also increase mortality in unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
sideeffects.monitor: Monitor blood pressure after a dose.
verify: May have increased mortality in UA/NSTEMI

sideeffects.text: Bleeding is the main adverse effect of every agent, and includes intracranial hemorrhage.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch for new neurologic signs and any bleeding; screen carefully against the contraindication list before giving.

sideeffects.text: Allergic reactions, with fever, chills and skin rash, occur mainly with streptokinase. Anaphylactic reactions can occur with the class.
sideeffects.monitor: A prior streptokinase exposure or reaction is a contraindication; choose a different agent next time.

verify: STK prior exposure or allergic reaction

sideeffects.text: Ventricular arrhythmias are a listed adverse effect of the class.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch the heart rhythm after treatment.

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
contra.text: Contraindicated with heart rate below 60 beats per minute and with atrioventricular block.

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
contra.text: Contraindicated with systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg and in acute decompensated heart failure.

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
contra.text: Precautions: reactive airway disease, systolic heart failure, diabetes and peripheral vascular disease.

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
contra.text: Avoid non-cardioselective beta blockers in asthma; avoid beta blockers in bradycardia or atrioventricular block (a dihydropyridine is first line there).

contra.drug:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
contra.text: Avoid in variant (vasospastic) angina: beta blockers may lead to worsened symptoms.

contra.drug: Beta blockers in acute coronary syndrome
contra.text: Caution with bradycardia or hypotension, heart block and severe reactive airway disease.
verify: Caution with bradycardia/hypotension, heart block, severe reactive airway disease

contra.drug:
Calcium channel blockers
dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine
contra.text: Contraindicated with systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg.

contra.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
contra.text: Contraindicated with heart rate below 60, acute heart failure and ejection fraction below 40 percent. Atrioventricular block is also listed; it is the non-dihydropyridines that slow atrioventricular conduction.

contra.drug:
Calcium channel blockers
dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine
contra.text: Precautions: concurrent beta blocker use (non-dihydropyridines) and cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) interactions.

contra.drug:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine
contra.text: Avoid short-acting agents, nifedipine being the named example.

contra.drug:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
contra.text: Avoid in bradycardia or atrioventricular block (a dihydropyridine is first line).

contra.drug:
Calcium channel blockers
dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine
contra.text: Decreased left ventricular function: amlodipine is the calcium channel blocker alternative; other calcium channel blockers are avoided.

contra.drug:
Nitrates
nitroglycerin, isosorbide
contra.text: Avoid in severe aortic valve stenosis and obstructive cardiomyopathy (older lists call these contraindications; the risk is hypotension).

contra.drug:
Nitrates
nitroglycerin, isosorbide
contra.text: Contraindicated with phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil): concurrent use may lead to hypotension, myocardial infarction or stroke.
verify: Concurrent use may lead to hypotension, MI/stroke

contra.drug: Nitrates in acute coronary syndrome
contra.text: Contraindicated with hypotension and with phosphodiesterase inhibitors. No mortality benefit, only pain relief.

contra.drug: Aspirin in acute coronary syndrome
contra.text: Contraindications: allergy, recent gastrointestinal bleeding, recent intracranial hemorrhage. (Clopidogrel is the alternative for aspirin allergy in stable disease.)

contra.drug:
Fibrinolytics
streptokinase; alteplase (Activase), reteplase (Retavase), tenecteplase (TNKase)
contra.text: Active bleeding or a hemorrhagic disorder.

contra.drug:
Fibrinolytics
streptokinase; alteplase (Activase), reteplase (Retavase), tenecteplase (TNKase)
contra.text: Recent surgery, procedures and bleeding: surgery within 10 days (including organ biopsy, puncture of non-compressible vessels and cardiopulmonary resuscitation); serious gastrointestinal bleeding within 3 months. These are older cut-offs: current guidelines treat recent major surgery, prolonged resuscitation, non-compressible punctures and recent internal bleeding as relative contraindications with different time limits.

contra.drug:
Fibrinolytics
streptokinase; alteplase (Activase), reteplase (Retavase), tenecteplase (TNKase)
contra.text: Serious head or facial trauma (current guidelines: significant head or facial trauma within 3 months is absolute).

contra.drug:
Fibrinolytics

charts.title: Antianginal Drugs Compared
charts.sub: Beta blockers, the two kinds of calcium channel blocker and the nitrates side by side, with the two vasculoprotective add-ons: how each works, what it does to heart rate and pressure, where it fits, what to watch and when not to use it.
headers: How it works (oxygen demand and supply)
Effect on heart rate, contractility and wall tension
Place in therapy and coexisting conditions
charts.notes: Reading the hemodynamic column: wall tension falls when the pressure the heart pumps against falls (afterload) or when the filling volume falls (preload). Nitrates lower the left ventricular volume the most (preload); dihydropyridines lower pressure the most; beta blockers and non-dihydropyridines slow the heart. Nifedipine, felodipine and the nitrates raise the heart rate (reflex tachycardia; amlodipine leaves it unchanged) while beta blockers and non-dihydropyridines lower it. Two cells of the original comorbidity table are deliberately left out (“prior myocardial infarction: avoid calcium channel blockers” and the diabetes row that makes non-dihydropyridines first line) because they are over-simplified and do not match current practice. An older overview also says aspirin and clopidogrel increase coronary blood flow; that is not established, so it is not repeated here. Patient education for nitroglycerin: store in the original container, traditional rule: replace tablets 3–6 months after opening (labeling uses the expiration date if kept in the original glass container), call emergency medical services if the first dose gives no relief after 5 minutes.

cells:
Beta blockers
metoprolol, atenolol (beta-1 selective); propranolol, nadolol (non-selective); carvedilol, labetalol (third generation)
Lower oxygen demand only; no effect on oxygen supply.
Heart rate falls markedly; contractility falls; systolic blood pressure falls; left ventricular volume rises.

First line in the absence of contraindications. First line when there is hypertension, a prior myocardial infarction or decreased left ventricular function. Also useful in anxiety, supraventricular arrhythmias and stable (compensated) heart failure.
Hypotension, bradycardia, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, fatigue, sexual dysfunction, nightmares, worsened claudication.

Contraindicated: heart rate below 60, systolic pressure below 100 mmHg, atrioventricular block, acute decompensated heart failure. Avoid all beta blockers in bradycardia, atrioventricular block and variant angina; avoid non-cardioselective agents in asthma.

Avoid rapid discontinuation (stop gradually; added background: rebound angina and myocardial infarction, with a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) boxed warning on several agents); dizziness and fatigue. Monitor heart rate, blood sugar and lipids.
verify: First line therapy in the absence of contraindications
Prior myocardial infarction: first line beta blocker

cells:
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine
Lower demand and help supply: mild dilation in areas of fixed stenosis and relief of vasospasm.

Heart rate rises (reflex) with nifedipine and felodipine, but amlodipine leaves it unchanged; contractility unchanged or decreased; systolic blood pressure falls markedly; left ventricular volume unchanged or decreased. Strongest vasodilation (four plus); atrioventricular conduction unchanged.

Added to a beta blocker when the beta blocker alone is not successful; also combined with long-acting nitrates. Chosen (as a class) for vasospastic angina, asthma, severe peripheral vascular disease and uncontrolled diabetes; left ventricular dysfunction is dihydropyridines only. First line in bradycardia or atrioventricular block. Amlodipine is the alternative in decreased left ventricular function.
Hypotension, headache, flushing, peripheral edema.
Avoid short-acting agents (nifedipine). Contraindicated with systolic pressure below 100 mmHg. Avoid calcium channel blockers other than amlodipine in decreased left ventricular function.
Dizziness; monitor relief of symptoms. Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) interactions.
verify: In combination with beta blockers when initial treatment with beta blockers is not successful (DHP)
DHP when combined with beta blocker
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (DHP CCB): heart rate increased
systolic blood pressure decreased (two arrows down)
Amlodipine vasodilation ++++, contractility unchanged or decreased, heart rate unchanged

cells:
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
diltiazem, verapamil
Lower demand and help supply: mild dilation in areas of fixed stenosis and relief of vasospasm; act on the heart as well as the vessels.

Heart rate falls; contractility falls; systolic blood pressure falls; left ventricular volume unchanged or decreased. Moderate vasodilation (two plus); atrioventricular conduction falls (verapamil the most).

Initial therapy when beta blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated. Chosen (as a class) for vasospastic angina, asthma, severe peripheral vascular disease and uncontrolled diabetes (not for left ventricular dysfunction). Avoid in bradycardia or atrioventricular block.
Hypotension; slowed heart rate and atrioventricular conduction.
Contraindicated: systolic pressure below 100 mmHg, heart rate below 60, acute heart failure, ejection fraction below 40 percent. Caution with a concurrent beta blocker.
Monitor heart rate. Dizziness and constipation. Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) interactions.
verify: Initial therapy for reduction of symptoms when beta blockers are contraindicated or are not tolerated (NDHP)
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (NDHP CCB): heart rate decreased

cells:
Short-acting nitrates
nitroglycerin sublingual tablet (Nitrostat) or lingual spray (Nitrolingual Pumpspray)
Nitric oxide raises cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), lowering cytosolic calcium: vasodilation. Supply: dilating coronary arteries, relief of vasospasm, antithrombotic and antiplatelet effects.
Heart rate rises; systolic blood pressure falls; left ventricular volume falls markedly (less preload).
Rescue: relieve acute symptoms and prevent effort-induced angina. Sublingual nitroglycerin for acute relief.
Hypotension (orthostatic), headache, reflex tachycardia.
Contraindicated: phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) and hypotension. Avoid in severe aortic valve stenosis and obstructive cardiomyopathy.

Store in the original container in a cool, dry place; traditional rule: replace tablets 3–6 months after opening (labeling uses the expiration date if kept in the tightly closed original glass container); apply or spray under the tongue; warn about orthostatic hypotension; call emergency medical services if there is no relief 5 minutes after the first dose.
verify: To relieve acute symptoms of myocardial ischemia
Call EMS if no relief 5 minutes after first dose
left ventricular volume decreased (two arrows down)
Store in original packaging, cool dry place

cells:
Long-acting nitrates
isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur), isosorbide dinitrate; nitroglycerin ointment and patch
Same nitric oxide and cyclic guanosine monophosphate mechanism as the short-acting forms: vasodilation, preload reduction and coronary dilation.
Same pattern as the short-acting nitrates: heart rate rises, systolic blood pressure falls, left ventricular volume falls markedly.

Usually an adjunct and not recommended as monotherapy; allowed as initial therapy when beta blockers and calcium channel blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated, otherwise added to them. Mononitrate lasts 12 hours (once daily); dinitrate 3–6 hours (three times daily). Useful in variant angina.
Headache, flushing, postural hypotension, reflex tachycardia; tolerance (tachyphylaxis).
Contraindicated: phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors. Avoid in severe aortic valve stenosis and obstructive cardiomyopathy.
Nitrate-free interval: patch or ointment 12 hours on, 12 hours off; wipe off the old ointment before applying the new one; keep covered with applicator paper.

verify: Duration 3-6 hours, dosed three times daily
Headache, flushing, postural hypotension, reflex tachycardia
Wipe off previous dose before adding new dose
Calcium channel blockers and nitrates can reduce symptoms

cells:
ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors
vasculoprotective add-on
Not antianginal: do not significantly affect myocardial oxygen consumption; may help prevent progression of coronary artery disease.
No significant effect on oxygen consumption; do not relieve symptoms of angina.

For coronary artery disease with diabetes and/or left ventricular systolic dysfunction; indefinite use after myocardial infarction, left ventricular dysfunction or diabetes; consider in all patients with coronary artery disease or other vascular disease.
Adverse effects are covered in the antihypertensive drug chart.
Pregnancy contraindication is covered in the antihypertensive drug chart.
Long-term protection, not symptom relief.
verify: Do not significantly affect myocardial oxygen consumption
Do not relieve symptoms of angina
Used in patients with coronary artery disease with diabetes and/or left ventricular systolic dysfunction

cells:
Aspirin and clopidogrel
antiplatelet, vasculoprotective add-on
Antiplatelet: used to prevent acute coronary syndrome.
No heart rate, contractility or wall tension effect is listed; they are preventive, not antianginal.
Aspirin for all patients with ischemic heart disease in the absence of contraindications. Clopidogrel (as efficacious in secondary prevention) for patients allergic to aspirin.
Adverse effects of aspirin and clopidogrel are not covered here; aspirin contraindications are in the next column.
Aspirin: allergy, recent gastrointestinal bleed, recent intracranial hemorrhage.
Clopidogrel is the substitute when aspirin cannot be taken because of allergy.
verify: Aspirin in the absence of contraindications
Used to prevent acute coronary syndrome
Recommended for patients allergic to aspirin
As efficacious as aspirin in secondary prevention

charts.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome Drugs Compared
charts.sub: What each drug given for an acute coronary syndrome does, when it is used, whether it is for ST-elevation myocardial infarction or non-ST-elevation disease, and its key cautions.
headers: Benefit and when it is used
ST-elevation myocardial infarction versus non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome
charts.notes: Three wording flags. (1) An older source says reteplase and tenecteplase have increased fibrin affinity; that is true of tenecteplase but not of reteplase, so it is stated for tenecteplase only. (2) It says fever, chills and rash occur mainly with streptokinase and urokinase; only streptokinase is treated as the antigenic agent here. (3) Its age, time and bleeding-rate numbers for fibrinolytics and the aspirin amount are left out because doses and percentages are not tested; know the qualitative points (fibrinolytics are for ST-elevation myocardial infarction and not for non-ST-elevation disease; bleeding including intracranial hemorrhage is the main risk). The fibrinolytic rows also simplify “activate only fibrin-bound plasminogen”: alteplase and tenecteplase are fibrin-selective, reteplase less so. Two more flags: beta blockers in acute infarction are taught here as intravenous then oral with an early mortality benefit, which comes from older trials (current practice favors oral therapy in the first day and avoids the intravenous route with heart failure or shock risk); and the fibrinolytic contraindication list is the older one, which current guidelines split into absolute and relative items.

cells:
Aspirin
antiplatelet
Antiplatelet; chew and swallow at the first signs of chest pain.
Reduces mortality and reinfarction; decreases recurrent ischemia, stroke and cardiac death.
Both: common therapy for ST-elevation myocardial infarction and non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome.
Contraindications: allergy, recent gastrointestinal bleed, recent intracranial hemorrhage.
verify: Common pharmacologic therapy for both STEMI and NSTE ACS
decreased recurrent ischemia, reinfarction, stroke, cardiac death

cells:
Nitrates
nitroglycerin
Vasodilator; sublingual until the patient is in hospital, then an intravenous infusion.
Relief of chest pain only; no mortality benefit.
Both.
Adverse reactions: hypotension, headache, reflex tachycardia. Contraindicated: hypotension and phosphodiesterase inhibitors.
verify: Start with SL therapy until in the hospital then IV infusion
no mortality benefit, just relief of chest pain
Nitrates - no improvement in outcomes, used for chest pain relief

cells: Beta blockers
Lower heart rate and demand; started early (older teaching: intravenous first, then oral; current practice favors oral therapy in the first day).
Smaller infarct size and less sudden cardiac death in older trials; the early mortality and heart failure benefits are not established today.
Both: common therapy for both groups.
Caution: bradycardia or hypotension, heart block, severe reactive airway disease. Avoid the intravenous route with heart failure, low cardiac output or risk of shock.
verify: reduction in early and late mortality, reduction in infarct size
Caution with bradycardia/hypotension, heart block, severe reactive airway disease
Common pharmacologic therapy for both STEMI and NSTE ACS

cells:
Morphine
opioid analgesic
Opioid analgesic for pain.
Management of chest pain unresponsive to nitrates.
Used in ST-elevation myocardial infarction; may increase mortality in unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
Controversial. Adverse reactions: hypotension, allergy.
verify: Management of chest pain unresponsive to nitrates
May have increased mortality in UA/NSTEMI

cells:
Streptokinase
fibrinolytic
Forms a stable 1:1 complex with plasminogen, exposing its catalytic site so the complex converts plasminogen to plasmin, which dissolves the clot.
Reopens the occluded coronary artery (reestablishes blood flow).
ST-elevation myocardial infarction (fibrinolytics are not recommended in non-ST-elevation disease).
Allergic reactions with fever, chills and rash; anaphylaxis; bleeding. Prior streptokinase exposure or allergic reaction is a contraindication.
verify: Streptokinase forms stable 1:1 complex with plasminogen
STK prior exposure or allergic reaction

cells:
Alteplase
Activase; tissue plasminogen activator
Recombinant tissue plasminogen activator: directly activates fibrin-bound plasminogen, so plasmin forms at the clot.
Reopens the artery; very expensive.
ST-elevation myocardial infarction, best early after symptom onset; not recommended in non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (bleeding risk exceeds benefit).
Bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage; the fibrinolytic contraindications apply.

Reteplase
Retavase
Recombinant, made in Escherichia coli cells; longer half-life than alteplase.
Reopens the artery; very similar responses to the other tissue plasminogen activators.
ST-elevation myocardial infarction only.
Same bleeding risk and contraindications as the class.

verify: Very similar responses and adverse effects

cells:
Tenecteplase
TNKase
Recombinant (Chinese hamster ovary cells) with substituted amino acids; longer half-life than alteplase, relatively resistant to plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and increased affinity for fibrin.
Reopens the artery; very similar responses to the other tissue plasminogen activators.
ST-elevation myocardial infarction only.
Same bleeding risk and contraindications as the class.

Used before percutaneous coronary intervention and when a stent is placed.

unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin (low-molecular-weight heparin)

Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome
unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
